Pedigree likelihood ratio

Source: R/pedlr.R
pedlr.Rd

The weight of DNA profiles for one family tree against another: is this child the son of that man, are these remains the missing brother of the people who reported him missing, are two people full or half siblings. Each tree is a table of people and their parents; people who are not typed (a dead parent, a missing relative) are summed over. The likelihood of the profiles is computed under each tree, marker by marker, and the ratio reported with its base-10 logarithm, the product over independent markers.

Usage

pedlr(ped, geno, freq, alt = NULL, mut = "none", rate = 0.001, range = 0.5)

Arguments

ped

The first tree: a data frame with columns id, fid and mid (the person, the father, the mother), one row per person; a founder has both parents missing, "" or 0. A parent must be a person of the table, no one may be both a father and a mother, and no one their own ancestor.

geno

The profiles: a data frame with columns id, locus, a1 and a2, one row per typed person and marker (labels; both alleles missing for a marker not typed).

freq

The allele frequencies: a data frame with columns locus, allele and freq (above 0, at most 1, summing to at most 1 at each marker). Every allele of geno must be listed at its marker.

alt

The second tree, laid out as ped; NULL (the default) for every typed person unrelated to every other.

mut

The mutation model: "none", "equal" or "step".

rate

The mutation rate per transmission: one number for both parents, or two, the maternal and the paternal rate.

range

The ratio of the chance of a mutation of d + 1 steps to that of d steps under "step": one number strictly between 0 and 1.

Value

An object of class pedlr, a list: locus, a data frame with locus, l1 and l2 (the base-10 log likelihoods under ped and alt) and lr, their ratio, for each marker of freq that someone is typed at; log10lr, the base-10 logarithm of the product of the ratios; lr, that product; and mut.

Details

A founder (a person whose parents the table does not give) carries two alleles drawn independently from the population frequencies (Hardy-Weinberg, no coancestry); a child receives one of the two alleles of each parent with probability 1/2, and that allele may change as it passes, by the mutation model: "none"; "equal", where an allele mutates with probability rate to each other allele with equal chance; or "step", where it mutates with probability rate to the other alleles in proportion to range^d, d the difference of the repeat numbers (allele labels must then be whole numbers), so one-step mutations are likeliest. These are the models of the Familias tradition (Egeland et al. 2000; Simonsson and Mostad 2016); a mutation matrix is used as it is, not made stationary, so a long chain of untyped people can shift the allele frequencies slightly. Markers are taken as independent (no linkage); the alleles not listed in freq at a marker are taken together as one more allele (under "equal", one more allele to mutate to), which leaves the ratio unchanged without mutation; under "step" the frequencies must sum to 1. Frequencies summing to within 1e-6 of 1 are divided by their sum.

The sum over the untyped people is exact: the alleles each person received from the father and from the mother are eliminated one at a time (Lauritzen and Sheehan 2003), which handles loops, inbreeding and any number of generations; its cost grows with the number of untyped people linked together and with the number of alleles, and a marker whose elimination would need a table of more than 2^26 numbers is refused. With mut = "none" and simple relationships the ratio equals that of kinidx() and patidx(); mutation turns an inconsistent marker from a ratio of 0 into a small positive one.

References

Elston, R. C. and Stewart, J. (1971). A general model for the genetic analysis of pedigree data. Human Heredity, 21(6), 523-542. doi:10.1159/000152448

Egeland, T., Mostad, P. F., Mevag, B. and Stenersen, M. (2000). Beyond traditional paternity and identification cases. Forensic Science International, 110(1), 47-59. doi:10.1016/S0379-0738(00)00147-X

Lauritzen, S. L. and Sheehan, N. A. (2003). Graphical models for genetic analyses. Statistical Science, 18(4), 489-514. doi:10.1214/ss/1081443232

Simonsson, I. and Mostad, P. (2016). Stationary mutation models. Forensic Science International: Genetics, 23, 217-225. doi:10.1016/j.fsigen.2016.04.005

Examples

# is AF the father of C? The mother M is typed too.
trio <- data.frame(id = c("AF", "M", "C"), fid = c(NA, NA, "AF"),
                   mid = c(NA, NA, "M"))
alt <- data.frame(id = c("AF", "M", "C", "X"), fid = c(NA, NA, "X", NA),
                  mid = c(NA, NA, "M", NA))
geno <- data.frame(id = rep(c("AF", "M", "C"), 2),
                   locus = rep(c("D3", "vWA"), each = 3),
                   a1 = c(14, 15, 15, 16, 17, 17),
                   a2 = c(16, 17, 16, 18, 17, 19))
freq <- data.frame(locus = rep(c("D3", "vWA"), c(4, 4)),
                   allele = c(14, 15, 16, 17, 16, 17, 18, 19),
                   freq = c(0.1, 0.25, 0.25, 0.2, 0.2, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1))
pedlr(trio, geno, freq, alt)
#> pedlr: 2 markers, mutation model none
#>  locus       l1        l2 lr
#>     D3 -2.90309 -3.204120  2
#>    vWA     -Inf -3.142668  0
#> log10 LR -Inf; LR 0
# the child's vWA allele 19 cannot come from AF without a mutation
pedlr(trio, geno, freq, alt, mut = "equal", rate = 0.002)
#> pedlr: 2 markers, mutation model equal
#>  locus        l1        l2          lr
#>     D3 -2.904393 -3.204554 1.996002003
#>    vWA -5.444349 -3.141802 0.004982566
#> log10 LR -2.002386; LR 0.009945212
